findings.summary: I₂C is a synchronous, multi-master/slave, single-ended serial bus invented in 1980 by Philips Semiconductors for short-distance intra-board communication. It uses only two bidirectional pins, SDA and SCL, with pull-up resistors, typically operating at 5V or 3.3V. The reference design uses 7-bit addressing, with rare 10-bit extensions. Bus speeds range from 10 kbit/s standard mode up to 5 Mbit/s ultra-fast mode, though practical speeds are limited by address space and a 400 pF bus capacitance restricting communication to short distances within a PC board. A microcontroller can control a network of devices using just these two pins, fewer than alternatives like SPI. The bus supports four operational modes: controller transmit, controller receive, target transmit, and target receive, using START and STOP conditions as message delimiters. SMBus, defined by Intel and Duracell in 1994, is a stricter I₂C subset promoting interoperability.

mechanisms.title: Two-pin bidirectional bus with pull-up resistors
mechanisms.explanation: I₂C uses only two pins, SDA (serial data line) and SCL (serial clock line), which are bidirectional and pulled up by external resistors. This minimal pin count allows a microcontroller to control multiple peripheral ICs. Data and clock signals are sent most significant bit first, with open-drain/open-collector drivers requiring the pull-up resistors to generate logic levels.

mechanisms.title: 7-bit addressing with START/STOP protocol
mechanisms.explanation: The bus uses a 7-bit address space (with a rarely used 10-bit extension) to identify target devices. Communication begins with a START condition (high-to-low SDA transition while SCL is high) and ends with a STOP condition (low-to-high SDA transition while SCL is high). After addressing, the master sends a read/write bit; if the target exists, it responds with an ACK bit. Data bytes are sent most significant bit first, and ACK/NACK bits confirm receipt after each byte.

unknowns: Exact maximum capacitance specification for ultra-fast mode transfers

Formal protocol semantics for data byte meanings in pure I₂C messages
Long-term compatibility of 7-bit vs 10-bit addressing in mixed-device networks
